I have been farming these 2 mu for 40 years, and I know what works. My household has five mouths, and with some of my family working off-farm, labor is tight—so I stick to the wheat-maize rotation that fits our land and our schedule. This spring, my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October. I will topdress urea when it greens up and irrigate three times from the well: at jointing, at heading, and once during grain filling if the sky stays dry. I will spray herbicide once in early spring, and if I see powdery mildew or aphids, I will spray fungicide or insecticide—so three pesticide applications in total. Before I plant wheat each autumn, I use the rotary tiller to prepare the seedbed properly. For the summer maize, as soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will direct-seed hybrid maize right into the stubble with no tillage—there is no time to waste between crops, and the less labor the better. I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress nitrogen at the jointing stage. Maize only needs two irrigations from the well, usually at jointing and filling, unless the summer is very wet. I will spray herbicide and watch for corn borers, so two pesticide rounds. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed from the local supply store—never gamble with unfamiliar varieties. If the weather is fair, I expect about 450 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize.
